title: Checkpoint: Building and Making
objective: After this level you can explain how modern materials and machines build cities and products.
summary: Tower cranes climb by adding sections to their own mast. Steel and concrete split tension and compression; elevators, TBMs, lines, robots and printers build and make.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale: how does a crane end up on top of a skyscraper?
cards.body: Nobody lifts it up there. A tower crane climbs, adding pieces to its own tower as the building rises. Watch how it does that, then put the whole chapter together.

cards.headline: The crane that builds itself taller
cards.body: A tower crane grows one mast section at a time. A climbing frame jacks the top of the crane up about 6 meters, opening a gap in the mast. The crane then lifts a new section into the gap, and it is bolted in. Meanwhile, big concrete counterweights on its short arm balance the loads on the long one, the same balancing trick as Level 82's elevator.

cards.headline: Building and Making, in three columns

items.label: Materials
points: Steel: iron with up to about 2 percent carbon (Level 86)
Concrete takes the squeeze; steel bars take the stretch (Level 84)

items.label: Building machines
points: Safe elevators made tall buildings practical (Level 82)
TBMs dig and line tunnels with concrete rings (Level 85)

items.label: Making machines
points: Assembly lines split work into small repeated tasks (Level 87)
Robots repeat taught moves; 3D printers add layers (Levels 88–89)

cards.fact: Two forces run through the whole chapter: tension and compression.
cards.context: An arch pushes its load into its supports; a suspension bridge hangs from cables in tension (Level 83). Concrete takes the squeeze while steel bars take the stretch (Level 84). Brittle cast iron is weak when pulled; steel is not (Level 86). Once you see squeeze and stretch, every bridge and building becomes a puzzle you can read.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 complete
learned: Why every structure must handle squeezing and stretching, and how concrete and steel share the two jobs.
How steel skeletons and safe elevators let buildings rise far beyond thick load-bearing walls.
How beam, arch and suspension bridges carry loads, and how tunnels are dug at the front and lined behind.
How assembly lines, factory robots and 3D printing each changed the way things get made.

questions.prompt: How does a tower crane get taller as its building rises?

options.label: A bigger crane lifts it to each new floor
It lifts new mast sections into a gap in its own tower
Its tower telescopes out using steam
options.rationale: A climbing frame opens a gap for a new section.

options.label: It is taken apart and rebuilt every few floors
options.rationale: It grows one section at a time.

questions.explanation: A climbing frame jacks the crane's top up, and the crane lifts a new mast section into the gap.

questions.prompt: What do a tower crane's concrete counterweights have in common with Level 82's elevator counterweight?

options.label: Both keep the machine from rusting
Both store electricity for the motor
options.rationale: They balance weight; they store no electricity.

options.label: Both balance the load on the other side
Both act as emergency brakes
options.rationale: Brakes grip the rails; counterweights balance.

questions.explanation: In both machines a counterweight balances the load, so the machinery works against only the difference.

questions.prompt: Building and Making recap: what did Bessemer's blast of air remove from molten iron?

options.label: Excess carbon, burned out by oxygen
Water trapped inside the metal
options.rationale: The oxygen burned out carbon and impurities.

options.label: All of its iron atoms
options.rationale: The iron stayed; that's what became steel.

options.label: The heat, cooling it into steel
options.rationale: The reactions released heat and kept it molten.

questions.explanation: Oxygen in the air blast burned out extra carbon and impurities, turning molten iron into steel.

questions.prompt: Building and Making recap: which pair of inventions let buildings rise well past five stories?

options.label: Tunnel shields and tower cranes
options.rationale: Shields dig tunnels; cranes came to help later.

options.label: 3D printers and factory robots
options.rationale: Those came long after the first skyscrapers.

options.label: Steel frames and safe passenger elevators

questions.explanation: Frames freed walls from carrying the weight, and safe elevators made upper floors practical to reach.

questions.prompt: Building and Making recap: of these three making machines, which arrived most recently?
questions.explanation: Ford's line came in 1913, Unimate in 1961 and the SLA-1 in 1987.
